annotations.description: The player chose to be on the draw instead of the play. In Magic: The Gathering, being on the play is almost always advantageous in constructed formats — you get to play lands and develop your board first, apply pressure earlier, and have tempo advantage. The reasoning stated ('play-draw advantage') is backwards: choosing the opponent to go first means YOU are on the draw, not the play. Being on the draw only gives you an extra card, which is generally less valuable than the tempo of going first in constructed.

annotations.description: Bottoming Green Sun's Zenith on a mulligan to 6 is debatable. GSZ is one of the most powerful and flexible cards in the hand - it can tutor for any green creature at any point in the curve and shuffles back into the library. The hand already has three 2-mana green spells (Badgermole Cub, Dredger's Insight, Malevolent Rumble) which are somewhat redundant in the early game. Spymaster's Vault is the weakest land since it enters tapped (no Swamp in play turn 1) and only produces black mana, which none of the current spells need.

Keeping GSZ provides a powerful late-game tutor that scales with available mana and can find exactly what's needed. Spymaster's Vault's activated ability requires creatures dying and the hand has no black spells to leverage it.

annotations.description: Playing Watery Grave instead of Bloodstained Mire is slightly suboptimal. Bloodstained Mire should be played first because: (1) It can fetch an untapped Swamp (like Overgrown Tomb or Watery Grave from the deck) without paying the 2 life shock cost if a Swamp is already in play, but more importantly, (2) Playing the fetch land first preserves flexibility - you can crack it later when you know what color you need, and it enables Revolt for Fatal Push. (3) The opponent has a creature (likely Badgermole Cub next turn), and having Revolt available from cracking a fetch land makes Fatal Push significantly better, able to kill creatures with mana value 4 or less instead of just 2 or less. Playing Watery Grave now means next turn you play Bloodstained Mire and can crack it for Revolt, but you could also just play the Mire now, hold it uncracked, and play Watery Grave next turn for the same mana. The key issue is that playing Bloodstained Mire first gives you the option to crack it on the opponent's turn for instant-speed Revolt + Fatal Push if needed, while Watery Grave doesn't provide that flexibility.

annotations.description: With Yawgmoth on the battlefield and Young Wolf in hand, casting Young Wolf is reasonable as it sets up the Yawgmoth engine (sac Young Wolf to draw a card and put a -1/-1 counter on Emperor of Bones, Young Wolf returns with undying +1/+1 counter, repeat). However, the player should consider whether casting Walking Ballista for X=0 first would be better - a 0/0 Ballista dies immediately but triggers Dredger's Insight (artifact leaving graveyard) and could be relevant. More importantly, the question is whether to cast Walking Ballista as a X=2 (4 mana) 2/2 that can shoot things, versus Young Wolf. With 6 available mana (Boseiju, 2 Forest, Overgrown Tomb, Swamp, and Spymaster's Vault is tapped), the player has 5 untapped lands producing GGGBG. They could cast Walking Ballista for X=2 (4 mana) as a 2/2 that can ping Emperor of Bones' +1/+1 counters or go face, while still having mana for Young Wolf. Actually, casting Young Wolf first is fine since they plan to use the Yawgmoth engine next turn. The sequencing seems acceptable, though casting both Walking Ballista (X=1 for 2 mana) and Young Wolf (1 mana) would leave them with more board presence. With 5 mana available, they could cast both - Walking Ballista X=1 (2 mana) + Young Wolf (1 mana) = 3 mana, leaving 2 open. This seems like a missed opportunity to deploy both creatures.

annotations.description: Psychic Frog is a 1/2 blocking Yawgmoth, a 2/4. Psychic Frog deals 1 damage to Yawgmoth (doesn't kill it) and takes 2 damage, dying in the process. The Frog doesn't 'remove' Yawgmoth at all — it just trades itself for 2 damage prevention. Meanwhile, Psychic Frog is summoning sick so it can't attack this turn, but it's a valuable card advantage engine that could be used on future turns. Blocking Yawgmoth with the Frog sacrifices the Frog for merely 2 damage prevention (taking 1 from Young Wolf instead of 3 total). The player's reasoning that 'Psychic Frog will survive' is completely wrong — a 1/2 does not survive combat with a 2/4. Additionally, the opponent has Yawgmoth which can sacrifice creatures and draw cards, and killing their own Psychic Frog in combat gives the opponent nothing, but losing this card advantage engine is costly. A better option would have been to not block at all (take 3 damage, going from 15 to 12), or use Fatal Push on Yawgmoth (the more threatening creature) while blocking Young Wolf with Psychic Frog (surviving that block as a 1/2 vs 1/1). Actually, Fatal Push on Yawgmoth requires revolt for mana value 4, and no permanent left the battlefield this turn under Qwen3L's control yet — but Polluted Delta could be cracked to enable revolt, then Fatal Push kills Yawgmoth.
annotations.actionTaken: Blocked Yawgmoth (2/4) with Psychic Frog (1/2), which kills the Frog while Yawgmoth survives.
annotations.betterLine: Crack Polluted Delta to enable revolt, then cast Fatal Push targeting Yawgmoth (mana value 4, killed with revolt). Block Young Wolf with Psychic Frog (1/2 survives blocking 1/1). This removes Yawgmoth permanently while preserving Psychic Frog.

The player should have exiled a high-value creature card like Archon of Cruelty from their own graveyard, which would allow Emperor of Bones to put it onto the battlefield with haste when +1/+1 counters are placed on Emperor (e.g., via Adapt). Archon of Cruelty entering would force the opponent to sacrifice a creature, discard, lose 3 life, while drawing a card and gaining 3 life - potentially game-winning at these life totals.
